passage:
Dear Ganga di,
You'll laugh at this. Our robotics team had to fill in a peer contribution form today, where each of us writes what percent of the work we did. I wrote 40%. Honestly, I thought I was being modest. I did the motor code and the wiring diagram, and I stayed back three evenings.
Then Prof. Iyer read the numbers aloud, without names. 40, 35, 40, 30. That's 145% of one robot.
Everyone went quiet. I'm sure Harpreet remembers her late nights on the chassis as clearly as I remember mine. I never saw her nights; she never saw mine.
Prof. Iyer said that from next week we keep a shared task log with dates. I grumbled, but I think it's fair.
Your brother,
Tushar

qa.q: What did the four contribution numbers add up to?
qa.a: They added up to 145% of one robot.

qa.q: Why did Tushar feel that writing 40% was modest?
qa.a: He clearly remembered his motor code, wiring diagram and three late evenings, while other people's hours were invisible to him.

qa.q: What will help the robotics team share credit fairly from now on?
qa.a: The shared task log with dates that Prof. Iyer asked for, so credit rests on records instead of memory.

qa.q: How might Harpreet see her own share of the robot?
qa.a: Harpreet probably remembers her late nights on the chassis just as vividly, so her own number feels right to her too.

grounding: A student realises every teammate claimed a big share of the work, adding to far over the whole, and accepts a written log.

passage: Chai stall, the night after our cultural fest. That's where it started, Sangeeta. I'm Lakshmi, and I ran the decoration team, five of us. We started saying who did what. I said I'd basically done the stage backdrop alone. Reuben said he'd done the backdrop. Farzana said she did the lights and most of the backdrop. Deepak said without his wooden frame there was no backdrop at all. We laughed, but it got tense. Each of us had been there for our own hours and missed everyone else's. Nobody was lying, exactly. This year, before we started, I made a shared sheet: every task, every name, every date, filled in the same day. Nobody argues now. Well, less.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi make before the team started this year?
qa.a: Lakshmi made a shared sheet with every task, every name, every date.

qa.q: Why did each person believe they had done most of the backdrop?
qa.a: Each of them felt proud of their own hours and missed everyone else's, so their own work felt like the biggest part of the backdrop.

qa.q: Why does the shared sheet help the team?
qa.a: Writing tasks, names and dates the same day replaces fuzzy memories, so credit is shared on facts and arguments shrink.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt when the others claimed the backdrop?
qa.a: Deepak may have felt his wooden frame was being ignored, since in his mind there was no backdrop without it.

grounding: A student recalls every decoration team member claiming the backdrop, and fixing credit with a written task sheet.

passage: I'm Nandini, and I share a hostel room with Sunaina, so I heard every chapter of her group's market survey. Monday night she said, "I'm carrying this whole project. I made the questionnaire." On Tuesday her teammate Kunal dropped by for notes and told me, quietly, that he'd done basically all the data entry, "like 300 forms." On Wednesday, in the mess, Ishita said she'd written the whole report and the others had just helped. I don't know who really did what. Maybe all three were right about their own parts and blind to the rest. On Friday Sunaina came back upset: their guide had asked each of them to write down their share, and together it came to far more than the whole. She sat down with a blank page and started a list, with dates.

qa.q: How many forms did Kunal say he had entered?
qa.a: Kunal said he'd done basically all the data entry, like 300 forms.

qa.q: Why might Sunaina honestly feel she is carrying the whole project?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel stressed and proud of the questionnaire because she lived through every hour of making it, but saw little of Kunal's data entry or Ishita's writing. So her part looms largest.

qa.q: Why is Sunaina's list with dates a good next step?
qa.a: A dated list shows who did what as it happens, so the team can agree on shares instead of each trusting their own memory.

qa.q: How does Nandini see the three different claims?
qa.a: Nandini doesn't pick a side, and thinks all three may be right about their own parts and blind to the rest.

grounding: A roommate hears three teammates each claim most of a project, until their shares add up to more than the whole.

passage:
Week one. The street-play team of four met in the college canteen to split the work. Jagdish took the script. Preeti took costumes and permissions. Nobody wrote anything down. "We'll just remember," Jagdish said.
Week three. Rehearsals ran late every night. Jagdish rewrote scene two at 1 a.m. and thought, I'm basically carrying this. Across town, Preeti was stitching the last banner after getting the police permission stamped, thinking the exact same thing about herself.
Week five, the day after the performance. Their mentor asked each of them to write privately what share of the work they'd done. Jagdish wrote 50%. Preeti wrote 45%. The other two wrote 40% and 35%. The mentor added it up on the whiteboard: 170%. Everyone laughed, then went quiet. "Next time," Preeti said slowly, "we keep a shared task log. With dates."

qa.q: What did the four shares add up to on the whiteboard?
qa.a: They added up to 170%.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish feel like the one 'basically carrying' the play?
qa.a: Jagdish felt tired and overburdened, seeing every late night spent rewriting the script but not Preeti stitching banners or chasing permissions, so that work felt like most of it.

qa.q: What choice did Preeti suggest after the numbers were added, and why would it help?
qa.a: She suggested a shared task log with dates, so next time everyone's work is visible on paper instead of each person remembering mostly their own.

qa.q: How might the other two members have felt when the mentor wrote 170%?
qa.a: They may have been amused and then uncomfortable, realising they too had quietly believed their own share was bigger than the others could see.

grounding: Across three beats it shows every member of a college team quietly counting their own work as most of it, until the shares add up to far more than the whole.

passage:
Chetan, before you fill in that peer-rating form, sit a minute. Let me, Saurabh, your old senior on this floor, tell you about my final-year engineering project, back in 2009.
There were five of us building a water-level sensor. I was sure I had done the real work: I wrote the code, stayed up the night before the demo. Deepak thought the same about his circuit board. Farida thought she had saved us all by writing the report. Nitin believed his contacts got us the lab slot.
Our professor made each of us write our share on a slip. Mine said 40%. When she read them out, the total was nearly double a hundred. I remember my ears going hot.
She said, "Every one of you is honest, and every one of you is wrong." After that we kept a diary of who did what, every day, signed by all five. It saved friendships.

qa.q: What were the five students in Saurabh's team building?
qa.a: They were building a water-level sensor.

qa.q: Why was Saurabh so sure of having done the real work?
qa.a: Saurabh felt proud of the code and the all-nighter before the demo, which were remembered clearly, while the others' efforts were less visible, so that part felt biggest.

qa.q: What did the team start doing after the slips were read out, and why did it matter?
qa.a: They kept a daily diary of who did what, signed by all five, so credit rested on a written record rather than on each person's memory, which kept friendships intact.

qa.q: How might Chetan look at the peer-rating form after hearing the story?
qa.a: Chetan may realise that a personal sense of doing most of the work could feel just as true and be just as off, and might check notes or ask teammates before rating.

grounding: A senior recalls a college project where each member honestly believed their own share was the biggest, and a written daily record fixed it.
